chapter_theme: Two songs at Sikkal (சிக்கல்): the courtesans who say 'put down whatever is in your hand', and a confession of singing false praise to misers to end poverty, with the plea to be looked on by Murugan instead; the praise names Singaravelan of Sikkal and its fragrant groves.
structure_note: 826 is a courtesan song; 827 opens with the flattering verse a poor poet sings to a patron, which is the confession.

826.reading: The poet describes courtesans with cane-sweet speech who melt hard hearts, startled glances, who spread their hands saying 'put down everything in your hand', pull a man's hands to their breasts and say 'untie my braided hair where I put the flowers', and asks not to wander in desire for such petty women but to be given the grace of the lord who spoke the word to Siva, delighted by the freed who praised him as the merciful one who pours out the three Tamils. The praise names Vishnu who cut the demons' crowns as uncle, the sharp vel that took Sura's head as he came spreading like a serpent's poison, Valli's breast, and the lord of Sikkal, where great ascetics of upright heart dwell.
826.nuance: கையில் உற்ற பொருட்கள் யாவையும் வை என கை விரிக்கும்: the courtesans' demand for everything in the hand is given as speech. பிஞ்ஞகர்க்கு உரை செப்பு நாயக: the teaching given to Siva, here without Om named; முத்தமிழில் தயாபர is how the freed praise him.

827.reading: The poet confesses singing to misers drunk on their wealth: 'kalpaka tree that protects poets, mountain of sweet virtue, whose arms press women's breasts, whose fame has gone to the eight directions, is there anyone in the world equal to you in friendship and truth, who is as generous to priceless Tamil words?', telling them his plight to end his poverty; a fool in great hardship, he now clings to Murugan's lotus feet as refuge and asks to be looked on with grace and given unfailing life. The praise names Murugan with the vetchi garland, the child of Himalaya's daughter, lord of the young forest girl and of the one Indra gave, Vishnu's nephew, and Singaravelan of lovely Sikkal, whose groves' scent carries thirty-eight kathams, who cut down the Asuras in battle.
827.nuance: The first half quotes the poet's own flattery, so the confession is in the genre of patron praise (செம்பாகமாகிய கவி), not of desire. வெறிகொள் உலுத்தர்க்கு என் பாடு கூறிடும் மிடி: it is poverty that drives the poet to beg from misers. சிங்கார வேலவ names Sikkal's god.

links.note: The Kural begs every beggar not to beg from those who hide what they have; 827 is the confession of a poet who did just that, flattering misers to end his poverty, and turns to the Lord's feet instead.
